title: Slain teen's father still searching for answers
article: Six months after his son Cyrus Green was killed by police, his father Henry Francois still has not seen the autopsy report which could help explain what happened.
As well, the father does not believe the son he raised matches up with how media portrayed him.
But in a home on Cold Lake First Nation, there exists a different series of pictures of Green.

They show a smiling young boy off-roading with his father or lounging on a couch with his brothers and sisters. "He wasn't a bad kid," said his father, Henry Francois. "The way I know Cyrus, he wasn't any of those things they said he was on TV."
To Francois, Green was a quiet boy who liked to play in the backyard. "He was always by himself," said Francois. "You ask me where Cyrus is, he was playing outside....he never was an inside person.
"He always talked about driving with me in my four wheel drive to his friends," said Francois.
Francois said Green's home life was a happy one. "It was like a picture perfect family," said Francois. "Nobody really fought, but the odd time they would have their little squabbles."
Green attended St. Dominic's school, something that his father made sure that he would do.

If children in his family didn't go to school, they went to work. But six years ago, Green moved to Edmonton with his mother. And Greene believes that if he were raised closer to home, things may have turned out differently for him.
The last time Francois saw him was four years before Green's death, when he met Green at his mother's duplex on the north side of Edmonton.
Francois said Green told him that he missed him, and wanted to move back with him. But there was something amiss, Francois said. "He looked lost."
Francois had heard that his son had spent time in jail, but he said that reports that he had an extensive criminal record were wrong.

Francois said he had only heard of one previous offence that his son had committed just before his death at the age of 17. From the account Francois heard secondhand from those who were with Green during his last days, the matter of Cyrus's death is far more complex than the initial media reports portrayed it as.
While his details are sketchy Francois said he spoke with a person who heard Cyrus yell that he had been maced shortly before the fatal shots rang out on Feb. 4.
Green lost track of his son after his meeting with him four years ago.
He said he could not afford to travel out to Edmonton, and he didn't want to hitch a ride and become a burden on his exwife's family.
While Francois called, Green never responded to any of his calls. At the time of his son's death, Francois was working at an oil camp.

His boss called him over and told him to call home. It was his mother. "My mom told me Cyrus was gone," he said. "I asked her, what do you mean, gone?" She told him that he was dead. He cried all the way home from his job site.
Because of the matter of his death, Green's body was subjected to an autopsy.
But when Francois asked for an autopsy report he was told neither the RCMP nor the medical examiner's office could provide him with one.
Francois and his family have been left to learn about Green's final moments through the media with the rest of the public.
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team investigated the mat ter of Cyrus Green's death to determine whether or not the police acted responsibly during the matter.
Gary Creasser of the Calgary ASIRT team handled the investigation, and he said the investigation is now complete, but the final results have not been released.
The Calgary team handled the investigation at the time because of a lack of resources at the Edmonton branch, he said.
Now Cliff Purvis, Executive Director of Alberta's ASIRT, must review that information before it can be released to the public.

Francois and other members of his family can only receive the information of the autopsy report when that information is released to the public at large, for fear that any information the family tells others may affect the outcome of the investigation.
Nevertheless, Francois said he still believes the police acted over zealously in how they treated Green. "They say he turned on them... but I kind of doubt that," he said. "Because that's not Cyrus."
